title: Voice Commander: a local voice agent that can’t be talked into harm
text: Local only

title: Voice Commander: a local voice agent that can’t be talked into harm
text:
The problem
Voice Commander operates a Mac for someone who can’t use their hands. You say “computer, open YouTube”, “click the third one”, “turn it up”, “commit my changes”, and it does it: opening sites, driving the browser, typing, clicking, adjusting volume, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and running terminal commands. Simple questions (“what’s 70 Fahrenheit in Celsius?”) it answers directly, without touching any tools.
Every model runs on the laptop:

Speech to text: Whisper large-v3-turbo (mlx-community/whisper-large-v3-turbo, about 1.6 GB) on the GPU through MLX, with Hugging Face forced offline. Downloading it is the only step that ever goes online.
The agent: Qwen 3.8 27B (qwen3.8:27b-mlx, about 18 GB) served by Ollama on 127.0.0.1, using its native tool calling. Any local model that supports tool calling can be swapped in with --model, but the client refuses any server that isn’t on the loopback address.
Speech out: macOS say, with three presets you can switch between by voice (“computer, use the british voice”): a flat monotone by default, British and American. The choice is remembered across restarts. Replies go in on stdin, never as an argument, so a reply like “-o /tmp/x” can’t turn into a say option.

So commands and audio never leave the machine.
A voice agent with control of a computer has an unusual threat model:

Anyone or anything can speak. A TV, a video the agent itself opened, a visitor.
The model reads untrusted text. Web pages, tab titles and terminal output can contain instructions aimed at it.
It holds remote-control rights. macOS Accessibility and Automation permissions are, in effect, permission to do anything a user could.

So the design starts from one rule: neither the model nor the microphone gets the final word on anything risky.

title: Voice Commander: a local voice agent that can’t be talked into harm
Voice Commander: a local voice agent that can’t be talked into harm
text:
The voice loop





flowchart TB
  A["Microphone<br/>(echo-cancelled)"] --> B["Energy-based detector<br/>cuts audio into utterances"]
  B --> C["Whisper on MLX<br/>(offline)"]
  C --> D{"Its own<br/>voice?"}
  D -- yes --> X["Drop"]
  D -- no --> G{"Gate"}
  G -- "stop phrase" --> K["Halt mid-turn"]
  G -- ignore --> X
  G -- command --> M["Local model<br/>(tool calling)"]
  M --> P{"Policy<br/>checks"}
  P -- refused --> R["Say why"]
  P -- "needs a yes" --> Y["Read the action back,<br/>wait for an exact yes"]
  P -- allowed --> T["Run the tool<br/>(fixed argv, no shell)"]
  Y --> T
  T --> S["Speak or show a short reply,<br/>open 8 s follow-up"]






You can interrupt it while it talks. The microphone and the assistant’s voice share one AVAudioEngine with macOS voice processing on (the same echo canceller FaceTime uses). As a backstop, any transcript that matches what it’s saying, or said in the last 2 seconds, is dropped, so its own voice can never become a command even if cancellation is imperfect. If voice processing can’t start, it falls back to ignoring the microphone while it speaks.
When you don’t want it talking, “computer, voice off” (or muting the Mac) switches replies to a small panel in the corner of the screen that fades after a few seconds, and “dismiss” hides it. Confirmation questions are the exception: they’re always spoken, and stay on screen for the full 30 seconds you have to answer, so you always know what you’re saying yes to.

title: Voice Commander: a local voice agent that can’t be talked into harm
Voice Commander: a local voice agent that can’t be talked into harm
text:
Keeping permissions narrow
Whatever app holds Accessibility and Automation, everything running inside it inherits them: every script, package install and coding agent in that terminal. So the permissions belong to a small Swift menu-bar app that launches the agent, not to Terminal, and the README walks through removing them from Terminal afterwards.
The agent also avoids needing them at all where it can:



Task
Route that needs no Accessibility




Open a site, video or playlist
open "https://…"


Volume
osascript -e "set volume output volume 70"


Browser navigation
Brave’s AppleScript dictionary


Wi-Fi / Bluetooth
networksetup, blueutil



Simulated typing and clicking are the fallback: they’re what a hands-free user ultimately needs, but they’re the reason the app needs Accessibility in the first place.
A --dry-run mode checks and shows every tool call without running it, and needs no permissions at all.

title: Voice Commander: a local voice agent that can’t be talked into harm
text:
How it was built
Test-driven throughout, red-green-refactor: 473 tests that run in under a second, in 57 small commits. The policy layer is kept free of side effects so it’s easy to test exhaustively, and the clock and model server are injected so timing and model replies can be faked. Python with uv, MLX Whisper for speech, Ollama for the model, AVFoundation through PyObjC for audio, and a Swift launcher for the menu-bar app.

title: Voice Commander: a local voice agent that can’t be talked into harm
text:
Known gaps
The safety rules are best-effort, and the README says so:

Anyone can still speak. A video the agent opened could say “computer, …” at the start of a sentence, and anyone can answer inside the 8-second follow-up window. Echo cancellation only removes the assistant’s own voice. Speaker verification is the next step.
Keyboard shortcuts inside apps that delete (such as # in Gmail), Return on a focused Delete button, and terminals inside editors such as VS Code aren’t caught.
It needs an Apple Silicon Mac with about 32 GB of memory for the default model.

title: Receipt OCR
text:
What it is
Petty-cash receipts for a group of restaurants. Staff photograph receipts, Claude reads the shop, date and total, staff check and tag each one, and a manager emails the month’s ledger as an xlsx file to the head of department.
It runs locally as a small web app for now; AWS comes next.

title: Receipt OCR
text:
What I built
Many small businesses in Japan still operate their monthly budgeting using data manually entered by fatigued shop employees who often aren’t trained in spreadsheet formats and standards, leading to the digital equivalent of a hoarder’s cluttered file system.
This project aimed to address these pain points in the simplest manner possible to reduce error at the entry stage by employees, and to reduce the headache for managers who would often spend hours untangling a spreadsheet that has had its formatting and save encoding ruined by inconsistent software across multiple computers.

title: Receipt OCR
text:
How it works

A model (Claude Haiku or Sonnet) extracts the shop, date and total from each photo, and the result is validated before staff see it.
An evaluation command scores the extractors against hand-labelled sample photos.

title: Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
text: Case study

title: Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
text:
The question
Atropine eye drops are used to slow myopia in children: the eye grows too long, and the drops slow that growth. They also dilate the pupil, as a side effect you can see without any special equipment.
So: can atropine-induced pupil dilation flag whether myopia treatment is working? If the children whose pupils dilate more are also the ones whose eyes grow more slowly, a pupil measurement could become a cheap, visible early sign of treatment response.
The data was a clinic’s export from an IOLMaster, a machine that measures the eye’s length (axial length) and pupil size at each visit. This page is about the reasoning more than the model. Most of the work was deciding what question the data could actually answer, and making sure the answer couldn’t be quietly steered.

title: Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
text:
Rigour
The pipeline runs in fixed phases, and each one feeds the next:





flowchart TB
  subgraph data ["Data (shared)"]
    direction LR
    A["IOLMaster export"] --> B["Clean<br/>test records, age rule,<br/>ID checks, de-identify"]
    B --> C["Quality flags<br/>flag, don't delete"]
    C --> D["Features<br/>growth rates,<br/>pupil split"]
  end
  subgraph analysis ["Analysis (per question)"]
    direction LR
    E["Locked plan"] --> F["Stepwise<br/>mixed models"]
    F --> G["Diagnostics"]
    G --> H["Sensitivity<br/>analyses"]
  end
  subgraph reports ["Reports"]
    direction LR
    I["Technical report"] ~~~ J["Plain-language<br/>report"]
  end
  data --> analysis --> reports







The plan was locked before any model was fitted. The question, outcome, exposure, adjustments, model and every sensitivity analysis were written down, dated and committed first. Any later change is logged with what changed and why, and anything decided after seeing results is labelled exploratory. Try ten analyses and report the one that “worked”, and the p-value means nothing.
Models were built up in steps: time alone, then age, starting eye length and sex, then the pupil terms. Watching coefficients move between steps shows what is explaining what.
STEPS = {
    "1_time": "AL_rate ~ years",
    "2_background": f"AL_rate ~ years + {BACKGROUND}",
    "3_primary": f"AL_rate ~ years + {BACKGROUND} + {PUPIL}",
}
Diagnostics paid for themselves. Residual and leave-one-patient-out checks caught two things: one optimiser reporting convergence at a clearly worse solution (so each model is now fitted with two optimisers and the better fit kept, with both reported), and one “patient” who turned out to be a staff test scan. Both fixes went into the plan’s change log.
Sensitivity analyses, all reported: around a dozen pre-listed variations, including pupil measured at the start of each interval, a population-average GEE model, one eye per patient, different interval rules, dropping flagged scans, and a cluster bootstrap that resamples patients, not rows:
def bootstrap_sample(fu, rng):
    rows = fu.groupby("Pat_ID").indices
    draws = rng.choice(list(rows), len(rows), replace=True)
    # Each copy of a patient becomes its own cluster
    parts = [fu.iloc[rows[p]].assign(Pat_ID=f"{p}#{k}")
             for k, p in enumerate(draws)]
    return pd.concat(parts)
Reported to the STROBE checklist, the standard for observational studies.
Test-driven throughout: about 120 tests cover cleaning, quality checks, features, models, sensitivity analyses and the report build, each written before the code it tests.

title: Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
text:
Two audiences
The analysis produced two reports from the same results. The full technical report has the models, diagnostics, every sensitivity analysis and the STROBE checklist. A separate plain-language report, three pages at most, is for the clinicians: what was asked, what was found, what it does and doesn’t mean for their patients, and no statistical jargon. Both come out of one build command, so they can’t drift apart.

title: Offline Japanese PDF Reader
text: Local only

title: Offline Japanese PDF Reader
text:
The problem
The main motivation is privacy. The documents I most need translated are government paperwork: tax notices, residence forms and contracts, full of names, addresses and income figures. Those are exactly the documents you shouldn’t be uploading to a cloud translator.
They’re also hard to translate well. Japanese municipal paperwork is dense: tables, amounts, era dates such as 令和3年, and legal thresholds where 以上 (“or more”) and 未満 (“less than”) decide whether you qualify. Cloud translators flatten all of that into a wall of text and lose the layout that tells you which box is which.
So I built a tool that translates them on my own Mac and writes the English back into the same boxes, tables and coloured cells. MLX runs the translation models and Apple Vision does the OCR. No document leaves the machine.

title: Offline Japanese PDF Reader
text:
Keeping the layout
For PDFs with a text layer, each block of text is extracted with its position, translated, and written back in place. English is usually longer than Japanese, so text has to shrink to fit, but blocks of the same size share one shrink factor, so a column of table cells doesn’t end up in five different font sizes. Fonts are subset to the characters actually used, which took the output from 30 MB to about 1 MB.

title: Offline Japanese PDF Reader
section: Not trusting the model with numbers
text:
Not trusting the model with numbers
This is the decision the rest of the design hangs on: the model never gets the final word on a number.

Amounts, formulas, limits (以上, 未満, 超, 以下) and era years are converted in code, before the model sees the text or instead of it.
Every translation is checked for changed numbers, operators, currency and glossary terms, and for Japanese left untranslated. A failed check is retried once.
If it still fails, the block is outlined in orange in the output, so a person knows exactly where to look.
An editable glossary of tax, legal and administrative terms follows the National Tax Agency’s English terminology.




The model’s output is kept, but the orange outline marks it for a person to check.

title: Offline Japanese PDF Reader
text:
Scans and phone photos
Pages without a text layer go through Apple Vision OCR. The OCR lines are regrouped into paragraphs, and the grouping respects table rules and changes in cell colour, so text from neighbouring cells doesn’t merge. The original text is then painted over with the sampled paper colour, or white text on dark cells, before the English goes on.
Phone photos needed one more step, and this image shows why:



Left: an angled photo of the form. Middle: translated as taken. Right: translated after straightening.


Translated as taken, the boxes are skewed and the English lands on top of itself. So Vision first finds the page and a perspective warp flattens it, and detections without a visible page edge are rejected rather than warped. Sideways or upside-down photos and scans are turned upright from the direction the text reads, and translated boxes are trimmed apart so the English never overlaps.



A scanned, image-only copy of the form, translated through OCR.


It works beyond forms, too. These are my own photos of public material, and they’re good examples rather than typical results:



Original photo, straightened, translated. The headline is wrong: スケートボードパーク誕生 should be “Skate park opens”, not “Skateboard weaving”.





A menu card with Japanese and the restaurant’s own English. The existing English is left alone; place names in the translation are wrong (糸島 became “Shijima”, not Itoshima).


The pipeline, end to end:





flowchart TB
  A["PDF or photo<br/>(photos: rotate upright,<br/>straighten, downscale)"] --> C{"Text layer?"}
  C -- yes --> D["Extract positioned blocks"]
  C -- no --> E["Apple Vision OCR,<br/>group lines by table rules<br/>and cell colours, paint over"]
  D --> F["In code: era dates,<br/>amounts, limits, formulas"]
  E --> F
  F --> G["MLX model + glossary"]
  G --> H{"Checks pass?"}
  H -- "no: retry once,<br/>then orange outline" --> I
  H -- yes --> I["Trim boxes apart, write English back,<br/>subset fonts → PDF"]

title: Offline Japanese PDF Reader
text:
Two models, an explicit trade-off
There are two local models, and the app says plainly what each one costs you:

Accurate: Qwen3-4B, about 5 s per page, uses the glossary. For forms and contracts.
Fast: LFM2-350M, a dedicated English–Japanese translation model, about 2 s per page, with rougher output. Fine for leaflets and quick previews.




The same form translated by the accurate model (left) and the fast model (right).


Timings are approximate, measured on my Mac. Full pages.

title: Offline Japanese PDF Reader
section: Private by design, even on a phone
text:
Private by design, even on a phone



The web UI: model choice, the built-in safeguards, and an upload box for PDFs and photos.


The Streamlit web UI only listens on 127.0.0.1. To use it from my iPhone, japanese-pdf-reader-phone on shares it over Tailscale Serve with my own devices only, and it refuses to run while Tailscale Funnel is on. off is a kill switch that removes the sharing again.




After translating, the app says how many passages need checking and previews the result side by side.





The same app on an iPhone, over the private tailnet.

title: Offline Japanese PDF Reader
text:
How it was built
Test-driven throughout, red-green-refactor: 199 fast tests, plus slow tests that run the real models when I ask for them, in 44 small commits. Python 3.12 with uv, PyMuPDF for the PDFs, Pillow and pillow-heif for photos, MLX-LM for the models, Apple Vision through PyObjC and ocrmac, and Streamlit for the UI.

title: Offline Japanese PDF Reader
text:
Limits

It’s a reading aid, not a certified translation. Check anything outlined in orange, and anything that matters.
OCR sometimes misses isolated single characters and can misread maths symbols: on the scan above, A≦B further down the page came out as “AIB”.
Vertical text (tategaki) and handwriting aren’t supported.
It needs an Apple Silicon Mac, for MLX and Apple Vision.

title: Snellen screening toy
text:
What it is
A webcam eye test you can run on your own computer. It shows a chart of classic Snellen letters, “Tumbling E” shapes or Landolt C rings, sizes them to how far you are from the screen, and tests each eye in turn.
The demo runs entirely in the browser: the camera stays on your device and no video is uploaded. It needs a webcam and a bank card (or any card the same size), which is used as a ruler to measure the screen and calibrate the camera.

title: Snellen screening toy
text:
What I built
Rapid deployable eye testing is still stuck in the 20th Century, with most online Snellen tests requiring a tape measure, a television sized screen, rock-steady seating, and a second pair of hands.
This project aimed to use a computer vision solution so lightweight that it could run in-browser, with the added benefit of keeping all patient data on their own device, so no strict patient confidentiality to worry about.

title: Snellen screening toy
text:
How it works

The same Python package runs on the desktop and in the browser. In the browser, Pyodide runs it with numpy and OpenCV.
MediaPipe’s Face Landmarker tracks the face; a bank card, held to the screen and then to the forehead, gives the scale for the screen and the camera.
Chart sizes come from the same geometry code in all versions, in device pixels, and font resizes dynamically as the patients’ head changes distance from the screen.
